Revenue Forecast 
5 
Q. 
Did the Panel update the Companies’ forecast Rate Year revenue? 
6 
A. 
Consistent with Department of Public Service Staff’s (“Staff”) position, the 
7 
Companies updated KEDNY and KEDLI’s respective Rate Year revenue 
8

9

11

 Q.

1 
calculate the forecast Rate Year revenue? 
2 
A. 
No.  The SRP used their own model to calculate the forecast Rate Year 
3 
revenue.  The SRP ’s model prices out Rate Year revenue at the service class 
4 
level.  In addition, the SRP used a different methodology to normalize the 
5 
historic data used in the ogive analysis.

7 
Q. 
Do the Companies agree with the SRP’s revenue price out? 
8 
A. 
No.  The Companies reviewed the exhibits provided in support of the revenue 
9 
forecast calculations included in the SRP’s testimony and noted a few 
10 
discrepancies.  The SRP’s revenue forecasts for both KEDNY and KEDLI

were based on the Companies’ corrections and updates sales forecasts instead 
12 
of the sales forecasts provided in response to IR DPS-798, which included the 
13 
corrections and updates forecasts adjusted to assume the NESE project is not 
14 
available.  In addition, the Companies noted that the SC-4, SC-7, SC-12, and 
15 
SC-13 revenues were not included on Exhibit ___ (SRP-3) and were not 
16 
included in the revenue at present rates used by the Staff Revenue 
17 
Requirement Panel to calculate the incremental revenue requirement.  The 
18 
SRP corrected these issues and provided revised revenue forecasts and 
19 
revenue allocation exhibits in response to IR NG-02 as shown in Exhibit ___ 
20 
(RDP-19R).

1 
Q. 
Do the Companies agree with the revised revenue provided by the SRP in 
2 
response to IR NG-2? 
3 
A. 
No.  The Companies’ revenue forecasts using the sales and customer forecasts 
4 
provided in IR DPS-798 do not match the revenue forecasts provided by the 
5 
SRP in response to IR NG-2.  Because the Companies and the SRP are using 
6 
different models to forecast revenue, it is difficult to determine the differences 
7 
between the two calculations.  As explained above, the Companies’ models 
8 
are more detailed, and the historic data normalization methodology was 
9 
different.  The Companies support the revenue forecast methodology included 
10 
in Exhibit ___ (RDP-2AR) and Exhibit ___ (RDP-2BR). 
11 
 
12 
Q. 
Do the Companies agree with pricing out the forecast of Rate Year 
13 
revenue at the service class level? 
14 
A. 
No.  The Companies’ revenue and ogive models are designed to price out 
15 
revenue at the rate code level, which is then rolled up to the service class 
16 
level.  The Companies believe pricing out revenue by rate code is a more 
17 
accurate way to develop the ogive analysis and resulting revenue price out 
18 
because the rate codes that make up a service class could have different usage 
19 
by delivery block resulting in slightly different total revenue by service class.  
20 
 
21

Q. 
What is the SRP’s recommendation regarding the Companies’ ogive 
1 
calculations? 
2 
A. 
The SRP expressed concern over the raw billing data used for the ogive 
3 
analysis (at 15).  Specifically, the SRP noted that the normalization of the raw 
4 
billing data does not accurately account for canceled bills and rebills and 
5 
recommended (at 17) that the Companies revise the ogive calculations to 
6 
account for canceled bills and rebills.  The SRP asserted that the Companies 
7 
could achieve a more appropriate normalization of the data by ensuring that 
8 
the allocation to each block step is not above the maximum possible or below 
9 
the minimum possible allocation. 
10 
 
11 
Q. 
Do the Companies accept the SRP’s recommendation concerning the 
12 
normalization of data used in the ogive calculation? 
13 
A. 
The Companies agree to revise the normalization methodology but propose a 
14 
different methodology from the one that the SRP proposes.  The Companies 
15 
agree that only removing the negative values in the upper usage levels could 
16 
have an impact on the ogive calculation, although relatively immaterial.  
17 
Therefore, the ogive calculations used to the develop the forecast revenue in 
18 
Exhibit ___ (RDP-2AR) and Exhibit ___ (RDP-2BR) were revised to include 
19 
any negative values so that in effect, the Companies are including the full 
20 


--- Page 9 ---
Case 19-G-0309 
Case 19-G-0310

impact of any cancels or rebills instead of potentially skewing the data by only 
1 
removing large negative volumes.

Q. 
Please summarize the NYCRDP’s comments on the Companies’ ECOS 
1 
studies. 
2 
A. 
The NYCRDP recommended (at 3) that the Commission accept the 
3 
Companies’ ECOS studies because they are reasonable and consistent with 
4 
past practice, and they allocate costs on the basis of cost causation.  The 
5 
NYCRDP also recommended that the Companies’ ECOS studies be accepted 
6 
as the primary guide for revenue allocation.  It also agreed (at 9) with the 
7 
classification of distribution mains as both demand-related and customer-
8 
related, as presented in the Companies’ ECOS studies. 
9 
 
10 
Q. 
What is the SRP’s recommendation regarding the ECOS studies? 
11 
A. 
The SRP recommends (at 27) using the historic ECOS studies provided in 
12 
response to IR DPS-504, instead of the Companies’ pro-forma ECOS studies 
13 
(using Rate Year information).  The SRP believes that using forward-looking 
14 
Rate Year information can introduce additional errors. 
15 
 
16 
Q. 
Does the Panel agree? 
17 
A. 
No.  The Panel believes that the ECOS studies should be prepared using the 
18 
costs, rate base, and physical units that are projected for the Rate Year, and for 
19 
which the revenue requirement, revenue allocation, and rate design will be set.  
20 
While the actual conditions in the Rate Year will be somewhat different from 
21 


--- Page 11 ---
Case 19-G-0309 
Case 19-G-0310 
Rebuttal Testimony of the Rate Design Panel 
Page 9 of 50 
 
these projections, the same is also true of historic year data – the actual 
1 
conditions in the Rate Year will be different.  In particular, historic allocator 
2 
values may not reflect normal weather, and historic costs may be different in 
3 
amount and type from the costs the Companies will experience and the 
4 
amounts they will recover in rates. 
5 
 
6 
The SRP acknowledges that when “very large changes in utility operations are 
7 
projected,” forward-looking Rate Year data can be used.  The Panel notes that 
8 
the filing of a major rate case means that significant changes are projected, 
9 
and it is important that the ECOSS reflect, as closely as can be estimated, the 
10 
conditions that will occur in the Rate Year and the amounts to be recovered in 
11 
rates. 
12 
 
13 
The Panel further notes that the ECOSS is easily rerun to reflect the 
14 
Commission-approved final revenue requirement, thereby reflecting the actual 
15 
amounts to be recovered in rates.  The final revenue allocation and rate design 
16 
cannot be done until the final revenue requirement is known, and rerunning 
17 
the ECOSS does not delay this process. 
18 
 
19 
Finally, an important goal of revenue allocation is to move classes closer to 
20 
the system average rate of return.  It is not possible to measure whether a

IV. 
Revenue Allocation 
4 
Q. 
Please explain the Companies’ revenue allocation process. 
5 
A. 
The Companies’ revenue allocation proposals move the returns produced by 
6 
each service class closer to unity (the system average rate of return) while 
7 
mitigating extreme impacts, a concept known as gradualism.  For both 
8 
Companies, a tolerance band of 25 percent was used to determine which 
9 
service classifications had a rate of return at present rates close to the overall 
10 
rate of return at present rates.  Classes with returns at present rates above the 
11 
tolerance band were given smaller percentage increases than the average 
12 
increase, and classes with returns below the tolerance were given larger 
13 
increases.  Some adjustments were made for outlier classes and to promote 
14 
certain goals (i.e., supporting interruptibility).   
15 
 
16 
Q. 
Do the revenue allocation proposals presented in Exhibits ___ (RDP-
17 
4AR) and (RDP-4BR) follow the same approach as the Companies’ 
18 
proposed revenue allocation presented in the Panel’s direct and 
19 
20

The SRP agrees (at 30) with the Companies that classes within the 25 percent 
1 
tolerance band should receive increases at or close to the average increase.  
2 
However, the SRP proposed that classes with historic returns above the 
3

7 
Q. 
Do the Companies agree with SRP’s recommendations on revenue 
8 
allocation? 
9 
A. 
As discussed in more detail below, the Companies generally disagree with the 
10 
SRP’s recommendations because the SRP’s revenue allocation, which relies 
11 
on historic year ECOS studies, produces results that depart significantly from 
12 
cost-based ratemaking. 
13 
 
14 
Q. 
Please comment on the SRP’s recommendation to use the historic ECOS 
15 
studies as a guide in revenue allocation. 
16 
A. 
As discussed above, the Panel recommends the Commission reject the SRP’s 
17 
use of a historic ECOSS because it does not reflect the amounts to be 
18 
recovered in rates and does not allow parties to measure whether a proposed 
19 
revenue allocation moves classes closer to the system average rate of return. 
20

Q. 
Are the SRP’s adjustments to ETIP and the Tax Reform Surcredit 
1 
necessary if a pro-forma (Rate Year) ECOSS is used as the Companies 
2 
have done? 
3 
A. 
No.  Those adjustments are not needed because Rate Year revenue at present 
4 
rates already reflects the roll-in of those amounts; the roll-in itself is supported 
5 
by the SRP.  Exhibits ___ (RDP-4AR) and (RDP-4BR), Schedule 1 
6 
demonstrates that the Companies’ revenue allocation proposals produce the 
7 
correct revenue. 
8 
 
9 
Q. 
Please comment on the SRP’s recommendation regarding the increases 
10 
given to classes over and under the tolerance band. 
11 
A. 
The SRP’s approach is flawed because it removes judgment from revenue 
12 
allocation and produces inconsistent results.  The SRP’s proposed increases, 
13 
especially for KEDLI, are inconsistent, because classes with similar returns at 
14 
present rates (for the Rate Year) receive very different increases.  In addition, 
15 
the SRP’s approach treats classes just within the tolerance band differently 
16 
from classes just over and treats classes just over the tolerance band the same 
17 
as classes significantly over.  Finally, because the SRP’s approach is based on 
18 
historic year data, it necessarily ignores a key measure of revenue allocation- 
19 
whether it results in classes making progress toward unity.  For these reasons, 
20 


--- Page 18 ---
Case 19-G-0309 
Case 19-G-0310 
Rebuttal Testimony of the Rate Design Panel 
Page 16 of 50 
 
the Commission should reject the SRP’s formulaic approach over the 
1 
Companies’ more balanced approach. 
2 
 
3 
Q. 
Did any of the SRP’s other recommendation affect revenue allocation? 
4 
A. 
Yes.  The SRP proposed (at 48-49) that the rates for the non-firm demand 
5 
response service classes reflect total bills that are lower than the applicable 
6 
firm service classes by 30 percent (Tier 1) and 40 percent (Tier 2).   
7 
 
8 
Q. 
Do the Companies agree with this recommendation? 
9 
A. 
No.  The SRP’s proposal to compare total bills for the non-firm service class 
10 
and the applicable firm service classes would affect the non-firm sales 
11 
customers (for whom distribution rates are only a portion of the total bill) 
12 
much differently from TC/IT transportation customers (for whom distribution 
13 
rates are the entire bill) and would produce significantly different results 
14 
between non-firm sales and non-firm transportation customers.  The 
15 
Companies believe their proposed rate design provides for attractive price 
16 
signals for non-firm demand response service. 
17 
 
18 
Q. 
Please summarize UIU’s comments regarding revenue allocation. 
19 
A. 
UIU recommends (at 35) that revenue allocation be evaluated using both the 
20 
Companies’ ECOS studies (which use Rate Year data and a customer-demand 
21

Q 
Please comment on UIU’s recommendation that the Commission place 
1 
boundaries around the relative percentage change a class may receive. 
2 
A. 
The Panel agrees that gradualism is an important goal of revenue allocation 
3 
and rate design, and explicitly reflected that in its proposals.  The Panel does 
4 
not believe, however, that any purpose would be served by hard and fast rules.  
5 
For example, if the overall increase is five percent, it may be reasonable for a 
6 
class to receive an increase of twice the average, or ten percent.  But if the 
7 
overall increase if 20 percent, it may create hardship for a class to receive an 
8 
increase of 1.5 times the average, or 30 percent.  The Panel supports the use of 
9 
boundaries that are developed in response to the specifics of each rate filing, 
10 
as reflected in the proposals it has offered in these rate cases. 
11

V. 
Rate Design 
7 
Q. 
Please briefly describe the Companies’ rate design presented in Exhibits 
8 
___ (RDP-4AR) and (RDP-4BR), Schedule 3. 
9 
A. 
For both KEDNY and KEDLI, the proposed rate design includes volumetric 
10 
rates that, together with the minimum charges, are designed to produce the 
11 
revenue target for each class.  For the classes served by KEDNY and KEDLI 
12 
with blocked rates, the rates reduce the slope (i.e., the ratio of mid-block rate 
13 
to tail-block) compared to the present rate design.  A lower slope supports 
14 
conservation by making the tail-block rate higher.  The Companies also 
15 
submitted an inclining block study (Exhibit ___ (RDP-11)), which analyzed 
16 
the bill impact of four rate design scenarios including an inclining block 
17 
structure where the tail-block rate would be higher than the mid-block rate.  
18 
The study showed that a significant reduction in slope would cause either 
19 
regressive bill impacts (lower usage customers would see higher increases 
20 
than higher usage customers) or a huge burden on higher usage customers.  
21

1 
VIII. 
Non-Firm SCs 
2 
Q. 
What costs are currently included in the gas costs for TC and IT sales 
3 
 
service? 
4 
A. 
For IT sales service, the cost of gas includes the WACOG adjusted for LAUF, 
5 
a merchant function charge, and a Tax Reform Surcredit.  For TC sales 
6 
service, the cost of gas includes the same components, which are all 
7 
volumetric based on usage, plus an average fixed cost of gas demand charge. 
8 
 
9 
Q. 
Do the Companies propose to change the calculation of gas costs for the 
10 
new non-firm demand response sales service class? 
11 
A. 
Yes.  The Companies propose to use the current TC cost of gas formula for all 
12 
customers in the new non-firm demand response classes, so that all non-firm 
13 
customers will pay the demand charge.  The Companies develop demand 
14 
charges at the beginning of each GAC year based on a cost of service study 
15 
that allocates capacity costs to each service classification depending on that 
16 
class’s usage during the annual period, the winter period, and the peak day.  
17 
The demand charge is the one component that is currently not in the IT cost of 
18 
gas calculation.  
19 
 
20 


--- Page 30 ---
Case 19-G-0309 
Case 19-G-0310 
Rebuttal Testimony of the Rate Design Panel 
Page 28 of 50 
 
Q. 
Do the Companies agree with the SRP’s recommendation (at 50) to use 
1 
ICOG instead of WACOG in the gas cost calculation for non-firm 
2 
customers? 
3 
A. 
No.  The Companies do not agree with this recommendation.  KEDNY and 
4 
KEDLI’s combined portfolios include having gas available for TC and IT 
5 
sales customers down to 15 degrees Fahrenheit.  The Companies manage the 
6 
KEDNY and KEDLI supply portfolios on a combined basis per Case 05-G-
7 
0903 to maximize supply and demand synergies.  Therefore, it would be 
8 
inequitable for any sales customers to pay only a portion of the supply 
9 
portfolio costs.  TC and IT gas costs have been calculated using the WACOG 
10 
since January 1, 2017.  The SRP states that the Companies have not created 
11 
adequate incentives to prevent non-firm customer from migrating to firm 
12 
service.  However, this recommendation would increase gas costs to non-firm 
13 
sales customers because the ICOG is almost always higher than the WACOG.  
14 
In addition, the SRP’s argument that firm customers are subsidizing non-firm 
15 
is not correct, because the times when the ICOG is likely to be set (e.g., the 
16 
coldest days) are the times when non-firm customers can expect to be 
17 
interrupted.  When this happens, non-firm customers have no cost 
18 
responsibility for setting the ICOG.  The main result of using ICOG instead of 
19 
WACOG would be to charge non-firm customers the costs they are trying to 
20 
avoid, reducing their incentive to take non-firm service. 
21

and install the necessary equipment within two days, the Customer 
15 
will have five more days to remedy the situation. The Customer will 
16 
provide proof that it has installed the necessary equipment and that it is 
17 
operable. If a Customer meets these criteria, amnesty for the violation 
18 
will apply. If the Customer cannot obtain and/or install the necessary 
19 
equipment within seven days, the equipment failure will be considered 
20 
a violation. Only one grant of amnesty for an equipment violation will 
21 
be allowed per winter season. Such grant of amnesty does not exempt 
22 
the Customer from having to pay any applicable charges, including 
23 
Unauthorized Use Charges or non-compliance Charges.

2

4

5

6

7

10 
economic choice for the customer, but they have several options: (i) fuel 
11 
storage on site, (ii) multiple smaller compressors, (iii) more fuel capacity 
12 
onboard, or (iv) use of public or shared fueling.

Request for Information 
FROM: 
City of New York, Justin J. Fung 
TO: 
National Grid, Rate Design Panel (“RDP”)
SUBJECT:
Energy Efficiency / Alternative Energy 
Request: 
53. 
With reference to expanding eligibility for Company-sponsored EE programs to non-firm 
customers, set forth on pages 33 and 34 of the KEDNY RDP testimony: 
a.
For each utility, identify the specific programs for which the non-firm customers 
will be eligible.  
b.
Will non-firm customers be eligible to participate in all programs identified in 
sub-part (a) above on the start of the Rate Year 1?  If not, please explain any 
delayed participation in such programs and the reasons for any delays. 
c.
Please set forth in detail the steps that the Companies have undertaken to assess 
non-firm customer interest in participating in EE programs; and any planned 
outreach or other efforts to create or modify EE programs to attract non-firm 
customers. 
Response: 
 
a.
Specific programs that would possibly be offered to KEDNY and KEDLI non-
firm customers are: 
Multifamily Program: 
The purpose of this program is to provide incentives to owners and managers of 
multifamily buildings to install energy efficiency measures.  This program will target 
master-metered multifamily facilities that receive gas service from National Grid.  There 
are several types of energy efficiency approaches that the Multifamily Program will seek 
to provide to customers, including: 
•
upgraded efficiency in design of new construction projects; 
Exhibit___(RDP-18R)
Page 1 of 10  


--- Page 681 ---
Form 103 
•
envelope measures in existing buildings; and 
• 
controls & operating systems in existing buildings. 
Commercial/Industrial Program: 
The C&I programs will be delivered by in-house program managers, account managers, 
and external engineering and mechanical contractors where appropriate. There are 
several types of energy efficiency approaches that the C&I programs will seek to 
provide to customers, including: 
•
upgraded efficiency in design of new construction projects; 
• 
envelope measures in existing buildings; 
•
HVAC controls and operating systems in existing buildings; 
• 
efficiency improvements of existing commercial facilities; and 
•
support for efficiency in expansions of existing commercial facilities. 
Targeted end-uses addressed in the C&I program include thermostat, boiler controls, 
steam traps, cooking equipment, insulation, windows, and spray valves, which will be 
installed directly by National Grid or its contractors when making onsite visits to 
restaurants and other relevant establishments. Custom incentives will be offered for cost-
effective measures not included in the list of prescriptive measures above.  
b.
The Companies did not propose a specific start date for non-firm customers to 
participate in energy efficiency programs; however, the Companies are not 
opposed to a Rate Year start date. 
c.
The Companies have not undertaken steps to assess non-firm customer interest in 
participating in energy efficiency programs, or planned outreach to attract non-
firm customers.

National Grid, Rate Design Panel (“RDP”)
SUBJECT:
Rate Design - Gas 
Request: 
54. 
Referencing page 59 of the KEDNY RDP Testimony, do the Companies intend to 
preclude TC customers with automatic switching equipment from electing to be served 
under the Tier 2 rate, which provides a lower rate in exchange for increased 
interruptions?  If so, please explain in detail the basis for eliminating that option for those 
customers: 
Response: 
 
The Companies do not intend to exclude customers with automatic switching equipment from 
choosing to receive service under Tier 2.  However, to be served under Tier 1, customers must 
have automatic switchover equipment.   
It should be noted that when the switchover to the new service classification occurs, all 
customers with automatic switchover equipment will automatically be placed in the Tier 1 
category.  If a customer does not want to continue their current level of non-firm service, the 
customer must formally elect to be served under Tier 2.

Request for Information 
FROM:

National Grid 
SUBJECT:
Interruptible Gas Transportation Rates 
Request: 
1. 
Please identify which investments in transmission and distribution systems proposed in 
the rate case are needed to support or improve service to interruptible generators? 
2. 
Has KEDLI conducted an analysis of the cost of serving the interruptible generator 
customers since the last KEDLI rate case? 
3. 
Has the cost of serving electric generator interruptible customers been calculated since 
the rates were established approximately 20 years ago? If so, please provide any citations, 
workpapers, etc. 
4. 
Will the presence or absence of the NESE project have any effect on the quality of 
service (e.g., frequency or duration of curtailments or OFOs) to interruptible generators? 
Response: 
 
1) KEDLI is not proposing any investments in the transmission or distribution systems that 
are specifically targeted to interruptible generator customers.  KEDLI’s capital 
investment plan includes projects to enhance the safety and reliability of the gas system, 
which benefit all customers by enabling the Company to continue to provide safe and 
reliable service and modernize its gas network.  These investments are discussed in detail 
in the GIOP’s direct testimony.   
2) No, KEDLI has not conducted any cost of service studies for interruptible generator 
customers since the Power Generation Collaborative in Case 16-G-0058. 
3) No, the cost of serving electric generator customers has not been calculated since the 
rates were initially established.  The Companies are awaiting guidance regarding the 
Exhibit___(RDP-18R)
Page 9 of 10  


--- Page 689 ---
Form 103 
appropriate charges for electric generators in Case 17-G-0011 “In the Matter of Review 
of Tariff Provisions Regarding Natural Gas Service to Electric Generators,” which was 
initiated by the Commission to review the required tariff provisions and rate structure for 
non-core gas transportation service to electric generators. 
4) The NESE project will provide more supply flexibility to support non-firm power 
generators that may reduce the frequency or duration of curtailments or OFOs.  The 
absence of the NESE project may increase the frequency of OFOs or curtailments due to 
increasing constraints on the Company’s system during non-peak periods.

STATE OF NEW YORK PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION 
 
--------------------------------------------------------- 
Proceeding on Motion of the Commission as to the 
 
 
Case 16-G-0058 
Rates, Charges, Rules and Regulations of KeySpan  
Gas East Corp. d/b/a National Grid for Gas Service 
 
Proceeding on Motion of the Commission as to the 
 
 
Case 16-G-0059 
Rates, Charges, Rules and Regulations of The  
Brooklyn Union Gas Company d/b/a National Grid  
NY for Gas Service 
---------------------------------------------------------- 
 
Reply Comments of National Grid  
to Comments of City of New York 
 
 
The Brooklyn Union Gas Company d/b/a National Grid NY (“KEDNY”) and KeySpan 
Gas East Corporation d/b/a National Grid (“KEDLI”) (together, “National Grid” or the 
“Companies”) submit their reply comments to the Comments of the City of New York dated 
August 9, 2019 (“August 9 Comments”) concerning the Companies’ proposed tariff amendments 
to modify their respective temperature controlled (“TC”) and interruptible (“IT”) service 
classifications.   
 
Summary 
 
In this filing, the Companies respond to each of the four points raised in the City’s August 
9 Comments.  First, the City misconstrues the Companies’ proposal with respect to the 
classification of customers with automatic-switching equipment.  Contrary to the City’s belief, 
National Grid’s proposal does not preclude such customers from Tier 2 service.  Second, the 
Companies disagree with the City’s recommendation to eliminate the current rule concerning 
“two-strike” customers being moved to firm service or terminated.  The rule is necessary to ensure 
that the Companies can provide safe and reliable service to its core customers.  Third, National 
Exhibit__(RDP-20R)
Page 1 of 10 


--- Page 701 ---
Grid disagrees with the City’s suggestion that the Commission reject the proposed requirements 
to allow critical care customers with two strikes to remain on the non-firm service classification.  
The proposed requirements for (i) an efficiency audit and (ii) the installation of a tank monitoring 
device are consistent with recommendations made by Department of Public Service Staff (“Staff”) 
at the TC/IT technical conference, and are reasonable suggestions to help improve compliance 
with interruptions.  Finally, the City’s suggestion for an expanded definition of “critical care” 
customers is too broad and renders the distinction of such customers meaningless. 
 
Background 
 
On February 7, 2019, the New York Public Service Commission (“Commission”) issued 
the “Order Approving Tariff Revisions and Directing Further Tariff Filings” in the above-
referenced proceedings (“February 7 Order”).  In that order, the Commission directed both 
KEDNY and KEDLI to, among other things, file proposed tariff revisions to blend the existing TC 
and IT service classifications and implement two pricing tiers determined by a customer’s 
switching equipment.  The order also required that the proposed tariff revisions address the written 
comments concerning critical care customers submitted in Case 18-G-0565, as well as Staff’s 
proposed solutions discussed at the November 27, 2018 TC/IT technical conference. 
 
Accordingly, on May 8, 2019, KEDNY and KEDLI filed proposed revisions to their non-
firm service classifications in their respective tariffs, PSC No. 12 and PSC No. 1.  Specifically, 
each company developed a single non-firm demand response sales service (SC 22 for KEDNY 
and SC 18 for KEDLI) and a single corresponding transportation service (SC 18-22 for KEDNY 
and SC 19 for KEDLI).  Each service classification will have two pricing tiers determined by a 
customer’s fuel switching equipment.  Tier 1 customers will be interrupted when the temperature 
Exhibit__(RDP-20R)
Page 2 of 10 


--- Page 702 ---
falls below 15 degrees Fahrenheit, whereas Tier 2 customers will be interrupted at temperatures 
below 20 degrees Fahrenheit.  Tier 2 rate will be lower than Tier 1 rate because Tier 2 customers 
will likely experience more interruptions.  The Companies filed further tariff revisions on August 
13, 2019. 
 
The Companies’ proposed tariff filings also propose a new definition of critical care 
customers.  Critical care customers are any non-firm customers that provide life-saving or life-
sustaining services (i.e., hospitals providing critical care, nursing homes, correctional facilities, or 
designated areas of refuge identified on an annual basis by local or state governmental agency), 
where public safety could be affected by a need to relocate the occupants.  Recognizing that certain 
customers provide essential services to the public, the Companies proposed to modify their tariffs 
to clearly outline certain requirements that will allow these critical care customers who incur two 
unauthorized use violations (two strikes) in one winter season to remain on the non-firm service 
class.  As part of the remediation plan to bring such customers into compliance with the applicable 
tariff, the Companies proposed to implement Staff’s recommendations made at the TC/IT technical 
conference to require critical care customers with two strikes to (i) complete an efficiency audit at 
the customer’s expense and (ii) install, at the customer’s expense, a tank monitoring device to alert 
the customer’s fuel oil supplier of tank levels.   
 
In its August 9 Comments, the City raised four issues concerning the Companies’ proposed 
tariff modifications to their non-firm service classifications.  First, the City understood the 
Companies’ proposal to exclude non-firm customers with fully automatic switching equipment 
from electing the Tier 2 rate and argued that “there is no rational reason to preclude customers 
with automatic-switching equipment, who may be the Companies’ most reliable source of 
Exhibit__(RDP-20R)
Page 3 of 10 


--- Page 703 ---
interruptible capacity, from electing more potential interruptions in return for a lower rate.”1  Thus, 
the City argued that the proposed tariffs should be revised to allow such customers the option to 
elect service under Tier 2.  Second, the City argued that the Companies should be required to 
eliminate the existing rule whereby non-firm customers with two strikes in one winter season are 
switched to firm service or terminated from any gas service for the remainder of that winter season 
and the next full winter season.  Instead, the City suggested that requiring two-strike customers to 
file a remediation plan, combined with the existing unauthorized use penalties, will provide 
sufficient incentive for customers who want to remain on non-firm service to comply with the 
interruptions.  Third, the City contended that the Companies’ proposed new requirements for 
allowing critical care customers with two strikes to remain on non-firm service should be 
eliminated.  The City argued that the requirements for an efficiency audit and installing a tank 
monitoring device will impose additional costs on those customers and will “not lessen the 
potential for an interruptible customer failing to interrupt.”2  Finally, the City proposed an 
expanded definition of critical care customers.  It recommends adopting a definition of critical care 
customers so that the list of facilities that fall under the definition aligns with the City’s own 
guidelines for critical facilities under the New York City Building Code.  Among the facilities 
suggested for inclusion, the City urges the Commission to include public schools that also serve 
as emergency shelters. 
 
For the reasons set forth below, with the exception of one issue that simply requires 
clarification, National Grid disagrees with the points raised by the City in their August 9 
Comments.   
 
 
1 August 9 Comments at 6. 
2 Id. at 9. 
Exhibit__(RDP-20R)
Page 4 of 10 


--- Page 704 ---
Point I 
The Companies’ Proposed Tariff Amendments Allow Customers with Automatic Switching 
Equipment on Tier 2 Rates 
 
The City believes that the Companies’ proposed tariff filing “preclude[s] customers with 
fully automatic-switching equipment from electing the Tier 2 delivery rate” and suggests that 
“[t]here is no rational reason to preclude customers with automatic-switching equipment…from 
electing more potential interruptions in return for a lower rate.”3  Pursuant to the February 7 Order, 
the Companies proposed two pricing tiers based on customer switching equipment.  If/when the 
two tiers are implemented, the initial classification of existing non-firm customers into the two 
tiers will be based on whether the equipment is automatic or manual switching.  Those customers 
with automatic switching equipment will be placed on Tier 1 rates, and customers with manual 
switching equipment will be placed on Tier 2 rates.  Furthermore, customers electing Tier 1 rates 
will be required to have automatic switching equipment.  However, after the initial assignment, 
customers with automatic switching equipment will have the option to elect service under Tier 2 
rates.  Customers without automatic switching equipment will only have the option of Tier 2.  This 
position was clarified by the Companies in response to the City’s information requests in Cases 
19-G-0309 and 19-G-0310, the Companies’ current rate proceeding. 
 
Point II 
The Existing Two Strike Rule, Which is Contained in the Companies’ Current Rate Plans, 
is Necessary to Ensure Safe and Reliable Service to Core Customers 
3 Id. at 5-6. 
Exhibit__(RDP-20R)
Page 5 of 10 


--- Page 705 ---
 
Under the current KEDNY and KEDLI tariffs, TC and IT customers who incur two strikes 
in one heating season are switched to firm service.  If, however, the Company determines that it 
cannot provide firm service to the customer, service will be terminated for the remainder of the 
winter season, as well as the entire next winter season.  After that, the customer will be eligible to 
apply for any non-firm service. 
 
As an initial matter, the Companies note that the two-strike rule is a part of the currently 
effective Joint Proposal approved by the Commission in the above-referenced cases.  (See Section 
10.2 of the Joint Proposal, which states, “The receipt of a second strike for any reason will result 
in the customer either being converted to firm service or having its service terminated”).  The Joint 
Proposal was extensively negotiated and agreed to by all the signatories, including the City.  To 
balance customers’ interests with the need to maintain the safety and reliability of the system, the 
Joint Proposal modified the two-strike rule to address situations where a customer fails to switch 
to its alternate fuel if a TC interruption occurs within 48 hours of the previous interruption.  In 
those circumstances, the customer does not earn a second strike.  (See Section 10.5 of the Joint 
Proposal).  Accordingly, to the extent the Commission determines the two-strike rule requires a 
modification that would deviate from the provision in the Joint Proposal, it should be done in the 
context of the current rate proceeding (Cases 19-G-0309 and 19-G-0310) to allow all interested 
parties to participate.   
 
In support of the its position, the City claims that the same rationale that the Commission 
applied to Con Edison in approving Con Edison’s recent tariff amendments in Case 18-G-0565 is 
fully transferable to the Companies.  That is not the case, however, as Con Edison’s non-firm 
service is substantially different from those of the Companies.  For instance, the Companies have 
Exhibit__(RDP-20R)
Page 6 of 10 


--- Page 706 ---
more than four times the number of TC and IT customers than does Con Edison.4  Consequently, 
the non-firm customers’ potential impact to the distribution system on a peak day is also 
significantly greater for the Companies than it would be for Con Edison.   
 
National Grid’s primary responsibility is to ensure safe and reliable service to its core 
customers.  National Grid’s distribution system is designed to meet the peak day requirements of 
its firm customers.  A key assumption in the Companies’ supply/system planning is that non-firm 
customers will abide by the terms of their service – namely that such customers will not add to the 
demand on a design day.  The design day requirements do not account for incremental demand 
from all non-firm customers.  Therefore, it is crucial that TC/IT customers switch to their alternate 
fuel source during interruption periods to maintain system reliability. If all TC/IT stayed on the 
system during an interruption, the Companies’ gas system would be in serious jeopardy of falling 
below minimum system pressure and not meeting the needs of their firm customers.   
 
Thus, an effective enforcement mechanism must be in place to ensure compliance.  The 
two-strike rule ensures that customers who repeatedly violate the terms of service are no longer 
eligible, at least for a certain period of time.  While unauthorized use charges provide a certain 
level of incentive, it is not enough.  Financial penalties still leave the fate of the Companies’ system 
in the hands of the non-firm customers.  The Companies must be able to exercise control over the 
demand on peak days to ensure it meets the needs of its firm customers.  The two-strike rule allows 
National Grid to manage the risk of non-compliance, and therefore added load, on a peak day.   
 
The City’s proposal to require customers who violate the tariff to file a remediation plan to 
address and remedy the causes of the violations does not address the Companies’ concerns about 
the safety and integrity of the system.  The City recommends no details on any such remediation 
4 Con Edison has approximately 600 interruptible gas service customers.  In contrast, KEDNY has 2,550 
TC customers, while KEDLI has 93 TC customers and 84 interruptible customers.   
Exhibit__(RDP-20R)
Page 7 of 10 


--- Page 707 ---
plan, and what would happen if a customer fails to comply said remediation plan.  At a certain 
point, the Companies must have the ability to enforce the terms of service.  For all these reasons, 
the City’s proposal should not be adopted.   
 
Point III 
The Companies’ Proposed Requirements for Two-Strike Critical Care Customers Should 
be Adopted 
 
The City recommends that the Commission reject the proposed requirements for allowing 
critical care customers to remain on non-firm service.  Namely, the City suggests that the 
requirements for an efficiency audit and installation of a tank monitoring device be eliminated.  
The City argues that the requirements should be rejected not only for critical care customers as 
proposed but for any non-firm customers for that matter.   
 
Both recommendations have been suggested by Staff during the TC/IT technical 
conference.  In fact, in its “Order Approving in Part Tariff Amendments” in Case 18-G-0565 where 
the Commission approved in part and rejected in part proposed tariff amendments by Con Edison 
to modify its interruptible service, the Commission specifically listed both Staff recommendations 
to explain why Con Edison’s proposed tariff amendments are not adequate, and directed Con 
Edison to file further tariff amendments addressing Staff’s proposed solutions.  The Companies 
submit that the proposed requirements are consistent with Staff’s recommendation in the TC/IT 
collaborative and should be adopted by the Commission.  While Staff broadly recommended these 
measures to all non-firm customers, the Companies propose that they apply only to critical care 
customers.  The remediation plan is intended to allow critical care customers to remain on non-
Exhibit__(RDP-20R)
Page 8 of 10 


--- Page 708 ---
firm service despite failing to interrupt twice in one heating season because of the public service 
role that they play.   
 
Point IV 
The Companies’ Proposed Definition of Critical Care Customer Should be Adopted by the 
Commission 
 
Finally, the City recommends expanding the definition of “critical care customers” to 
include additional facilities that are “essential to public health, safety, and welfare.”  As an initial 
matter, the Companies submit that its proposed definition of critical care customers is adequate.  
The purpose of designating a subset of non-firm customers as critical care customers is to 
recognize the necessity of continued gas service to certain facilities providing essential public 
services and balancing that consideration against the Companies’ utmost priority of maintaining 
system reliability.  Therefore, critical care customers must be defined such that it captures the key 
population but also is narrow enough to minimize the added peak demand.  The City’s definition 
of critical care customers is so broad that it would capture a significant portion of the Companies’ 
population of non-firm customers.  If all such customers remained on the Companies’ gas system 
during an interruption, the Companies will likely experience serious supply/system issues.   
 
While the Companies do not think the definition should be strictly limited to its proposal 
and are open to additional considerations, the City’s suggestion is overly broad.  Most notably, the 
City suggests that “critical care” customers should include public schools that also serve as 
emergency shelters.  The Companies are amenable to providing the critical care designation to 
such schools only when they are serving the alternate purpose of an emergency shelter, but not 
when they are simply operating as a school.

Finally, the Companies disagree with the City’s suggestion that the Commission align the 
Companies’ definition of critical care customers with the City’s guidelines under the New York 
City Building Code.  In addition to the fact that the list is too broad, the City provides no reasonable 
basis as to why such standards should also apply to KEDLI, whose service territory includes areas 
outside of New York City. 
 
Conclusion 
 
For the reasons set forth above, National Grid disagrees with the City’s proposed 
modifications/elimination of certain tariff provisions relating to the Companies’ non-firm service 
classifications.  The Companies respectfully request that the Commission approve the Companies’ 
May 8, 2019 filing without modification.
